query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor, targeted alloying addition during alloy synthesis to trigger in‐situ formation of coherent nanoprecipitates along the lamellar colony interfaces will improve interfacial connectivity and dislocation transmission. This intervention is expected to alleviate dislocation pile‐ups (and thereby local stress concentrations) that are responsible for microcracking and brittle failure, leading to improved room-temperature tensile ductility while maintaining or even increasing the alloy’s strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical, dual-phase lamellar microstructure (e.g., alternating soft FCC and hard B2 phases) that exhibits brittle room-temperature behavior due to dislocation pile-ups at the semi-coherent or incoherent internal boundaries.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small concentration of a selected alloying element (for example, Cr or a similar element) during casting and subsequent processing that drives a controlled, uniform precipitation of coherent nanoprecipitates specifically at the internal lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: Heat treatment conditions should be optimized to promote the formation and retention of the coherent precipitates, followed by room temperature tensile testing under conventional strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly distributed coherent nanoprecipitates forming at the lamellar colony interfaces, which act as bridges for dislocation motion and reduce local stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: The coherent interfaces provided by the nanoprecipitates ease the transmission of dislocations across the colony boundaries and reduce the formation of dislocation pile-ups. This both retards premature microcracking and adds a precipitation-strengthening effect, thereby resolving the strength–ductility trade-off at room temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA is predicted to exhibit enhanced tensile ductility (i.e., higher elongation to failure) and reduced brittleness while retaining or slightly increasing its yield and ultimate tensile strength compared to the untreated material.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy showing dual-phase lamellar colonies with limited room-temperature tensile ductility due to stress concentrations created by dislocation pile-ups at less coherent internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is anticipated under room-temperature tensile conditions and conventional strain rates; its impact under extreme temperatures or very high strain rates remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The choice and optimal concentration of the minor alloying element, and whether the resulting precipitates are fully coherent to achieve the desired reduction in dislocation pile-ups, remain to be determined through systematic experimental studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the eutectic HEA: one batch with the minor alloying addition intended to induce coherent nanoprecipitate formation and a control batch without the addition. Subject both batches to identical processing and heat treatment conditions designed to develop the lamellar microstructure. Carry out detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM to assess nanoprecipitate coherence and distribution) and perform room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
TEM observations of dislocation structures and nanoprecipitate coherence at colony interfaces
Quantitative analysis of dislocation pile-ups near interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy modified with the minor alloying addition does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility (and/or retains similar or lower strength) compared to the control, or if TEM analysis shows no reduction in dislocation pile-ups at the lamellar boundaries, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Abstract Concurrent strength–ductility improvement of HfMoTaTiZr is achieved via Cr addition and the underlying strengthening mechanism was discussed. 4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase. The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 535.8 Hv 0.3 , 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr. The yield strength and fracture strain of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 reach 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa and 14.0 ± 2.9%, respectively, 207.5 MPa and 20.6% higher than HfMoTaTiZr. Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength and the formation of a reticulated structure of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 results in the improvement in ductility.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
